items.bodyEn: Ishiyakushi was not among the stations named in 1601. The shogunate added it in 1616 to break up the long stage between Yokkaichi and Kameyama. It stayed small: the 1843 survey lists fifteen inns and fewer than a thousand residents. The town took its name from Ishiyakushi-ji, whose principal image is a Yakushi Buddha carved into a natural boulder.
items.sourceNote: 東海道宿村大概帳 (1843): Ishiyakushi-juku, 15 hatago, 991 residents; est. 元和2 (1616)

items.bodyEn: 薬, medicine, wears the grass crown 艹 because the first medicines were herbs; the Shuowen Jiezi defines it as 'the plant that treats illness.' Beneath sits 楽, music or pleasure, there chiefly for its sound, though learners may read it as relief. 薬師, the Master of Medicine, is the healing Buddha who gave this post town its name.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi (説文解字), entry 藥: 治病艸, 从艸樂聲

items.titleEn: The Buddha With a Medicine Jar
items.bodyEn: Yakushi Nyorai, the Medicine Buddha, vowed to heal body and mind and is shown holding a small jar of medicine in his left hand. His worship reached Japan by the seventh century; Nara's Yakushi-ji was founded in 680 to pray for an empress's recovery. Tōkaidō travelers stopped at Ishiyakushi's stone image to ask for sound feet and good health.
items.sourceNote: Nihon Shoki: Yakushi-ji vowed 680 by Emperor Tenmu; Ishiyakushi-ji stone honzon

items.titleEn: まい, Heir of まじ
items.bodyEn: The 〜まい of this station descends from classical まじ, which marked negative guesses and negative resolve. Its form まじき wore down in medieval speech to まじい and then まい. Modern Japanese keeps まい for firm written refusals, 二度と行くまい, and for literary conjecture, 雨は降るまい, while everyday talk prefers ないつもりだ and ないだろう.
items.sourceNote: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten (Shōgakukan), entry まい: 「まじ」の連体形「まじき」→「まじい」→「まい」
